questions.question: Explain the reasons American leaders gave for deciding to use the atomic bombs.
questions.expected_answer: Truman learned of the bomb in April 1945; the Interim Committee recommended use on a war plant surrounded by homes without warning, and the Target Committee chose unbombed cities (Kyoto removed by Stimson). The main reason was to end the war quickly and avoid an invasion (Operation Downfall, November 1945) after the huge losses at Iwo Jima and Okinawa, forcing unconditional surrender. Other possible motives: justifying the 2 billion-dollar cost, impressing the Soviet Union and limiting its gains (Byrnes), and wartime hostility and racism.

questions.question: Present the arguments that the bombings were justified.
questions.expected_answer: They ended the war without an invasion that planners feared would cost tens or hundreds of thousands of American lives and far more Japanese lives (Stimson's 1947 claim of over a million casualties); Japan's leaders were preparing a final battle and remained deadlocked even after Hiroshima, with an attempted coup; prisoners, forced labourers and civilians in occupied Asia were dying weekly; city bombing was already part of total war (Tokyo firebombing about 100 000 dead); many POWs, including van der Post, believed it saved them.

questions.question: Present the arguments that the bombings were not justified, referring to alternatives proposed at the time.
questions.expected_answer: They deliberately killed civilians (about 140 000 in Hiroshima and 74 000 in Nagasaki by end of 1945) with lasting radiation effects; Japan was blockaded, beaten and seeking Soviet mediation; the 1946 Strategic Bombing Survey said Japan would probably have surrendered before 1 November; Leahy and Eisenhower expressed doubts. Alternatives: demonstration (Franck Report, June 1945; Szilard petition), assuring the emperor's position, waiting for Soviet entry. Nagasaki came only three days later. Revisionists (Alperovitz) argue atomic diplomacy against the USSR.
